editions.title: Nscale loses Microsoft anchor as AI infrastructure jitters deepen
editions.notification: Microsoft reportedly walks away from Nscale's Essex data centre weeks before its New York IPO.
editions.intro:
The biggest story is a setback for Nscale, the British AI infrastructure firm. The Telegraph reports that Microsoft has pulled out as anchor tenant of its Loughton data centre in Essex, where grid power is reportedly not due until the 2030s. The news lands just after Nscale filed for a New York IPO under the ticker NSCL, with a float that could value it at up to $35bn. Microsoft and Anthropic make up about 85% of its contracts, so investors will watch delivery schedules closely. Nscale says it remains committed to Loughton and that its Microsoft relationship is strong. Microsoft has not commented.

The wider backdrop is a broad selloff in AI-linked shares. Japanese stocks fell as chip names led declines, Korean markets were hit hard, and South Korea's main pension fund reportedly lost about $137bn. Concern about whether AI spending will pay off also weighed on Oracle, Nvidia and neocloud peers. Analysts say Magnificent Seven earnings may test whether hyperscaler spending confidence holds. Meanwhile, the OpenAI Stargate project reportedly faces major obstacles, and Elon Musk again mocked the plan.

There are some firmer signals. Nvidia shares were set to end a three-day losing streak on a report that ByteDance and Tencent have each received H200 chips, and reports say Samsung and SK hynix may unveil a very large multi-year investment plan. Apple's iPhone Duo is dominating headlines, with supply strain, delayed shipping dates and a battery figure now confirmed, while Apple's AI features are reportedly set for China in December.

top_stories.title: Microsoft reportedly quits Nscale's Essex AI site ahead of IPO
top_stories.summary: The Telegraph reports Microsoft has ended its anchor agreement for Nscale's Loughton data centre, where grid power reportedly will not arrive until the 2030s. Nscale says it remains committed and is exploring alternative power. The move comes as the company seeks a New York listing that could value it at up to $35bn, with Microsoft and Anthropic providing about 85% of contracts.

top_stories.title: Stargate project reportedly hits turbulence as AI spending doubts grow
top_stories.summary: The Information reports OpenAI's $500bn Stargate initiative has stalled, with the Oracle-SoftBank venture reportedly not yet building. CNBC reports OpenAI now plans $600bn of infrastructure spending through 2030, down from $1.4tn touted earlier. Musk responded with 'Hardware is hard'.

top_stories.title: H200 chips reportedly reach ByteDance and Tencent
top_stories.summary: A Financial Times report says ByteDance and Tencent have each received about 10,000 H200 processors, with US clearance for larger purchases. Beijing wants most chips kept outside mainland China, and Nvidia reportedly holds around 500,000 H200 units, which helped lift its shares.

top_stories.title: Nvidia reportedly steers custom HBM base dies to TSMC 3nm
top_stories.summary: Seoul Economic Daily reports Nvidia asked Samsung, SK hynix and Micron to make custom HBM base dies on TSMC's 3nm process, with Samsung reportedly agreeing. The report cites TSMC yields above 90%. None of the companies has confirmed the arrangement.

top_stories.title: Samsung and SK hynix reportedly plan $1.3tn investment push
top_stories.summary: Korea Economic Daily reports the two chipmakers may announce up to 2,000 trillion won in ten-year investment, possibly at a government briefing. Samsung shares fell 4% on the reports, which come as AI-driven HBM demand remains strong.

top_stories.title: Google's Gemini 3.5 Pro reportedly months behind schedule
top_stories.summary: Bloomberg reports Gemini 3.5 Pro has fallen short of internal coding expectations and is months late, raising competitive concerns against Anthropic and OpenAI. Alphabet shares fell nearly 4.5% before recovering some losses after hours. Google says it is testing the model with partners.

top_stories.title: Apple Intelligence reportedly due in China in December
top_stories.summary: Bloomberg reports Apple plans to bring a limited Apple Intelligence version to mainland China with iOS 27.3 in December, after permits were granted. China is roughly 17% to 20% of Apple's revenue, so the rollout matters for sales outside the US.

editions.title: Microsoft quits Nscale site as AI trade wobbles and iPhone Duo supply strains
editions.intro:
The biggest story is a reported setback for Nscale, the British AI cloud startup. The Telegraph reports that Microsoft has pulled out of a deal to anchor Nscale's first UK data centre in Loughton, Essex, weeks before Nscale's planned IPO of up to $3bn. Nscale says it remains committed to the site and that its Microsoft relationship is strong, and Microsoft has not commented. The report lands as investors grow wary of neocloud firms, and CoreWeave shares were marked down in coverage of the story.

The wider backdrop is a deepening selloff in US tech shares. Bloomberg reports that this is exposing weak spots in Asia's AI "picks and shovels" suppliers, with rising financing costs threatening data-centre and hardware spending. The FT also argues that America's roughly $10tn AI infrastructure build-out is running into physical constraints. Against that, SemiAnalysis says more than 300 local data-centre moratoriums have delayed only a few projects so far. Meta's earnings, previewed by the FT as a test of confidence in AI spending, are the next major read-across.

Apple dominated the rest of the day's flow. The iPhone Duo, its first foldable, is reportedly sold out into January, with staff told walk-in buyers are unlikely to get stock on launch day, and Gurman calls the staggered pre-order rollout a "major mistake". Apple's EU energy label put the device's battery at 4,883 mAh. Rumours also point to a touchscreen MacBook and a HomeView smart display with a robotic arm, with a possible retail refresh on 6 November. Most of these remain unconfirmed.

top_stories.summary: Apple Store staff reportedly told customers without pre-orders to expect no launch-day stock. Apple says demand is extraordinary, and shipping estimates have slipped to around late January in most countries.

editions.title: Microsoft Walks Away From Nscale Site as Neocloud Nerves Grow
editions.intro:
The biggest story of the day is Microsoft's reported withdrawal from an anchor deal for Nscale's first British data centre in Loughton, Essex. The Telegraph says Microsoft has pulled out weeks before the AI cloud startup's planned IPO, which is reported to seek up to $3bn. Nscale says it remains committed to the site and that its Microsoft relationship is strong, while Microsoft has not commented. Grid connection delays at the site were also reported, and the story is being read as a sign of wider caution toward neocloud firms.

That caution fed into a broader theme of AI-trade nerves. Bloomberg reports that a deepening selloff in US tech shares is exposing weak spots in Asia's AI supply chain, with rising financing costs threatening data-centre and hardware spending. The Financial Times, meanwhile, argues America's roughly $10tn AI infrastructure build-out is running into physical limits of power, equipment and money. Investors will look to Meta's earnings next, which the FT frames as a test of whether confidence in the AI spending boom can be restored.

Elsewhere, Ericsson beat expectations with third-quarter adjusted EBITA of SEK 10.1bn against a consensus of SEK 7.93bn, and its shares rose as much as 11% in Stockholm. On the chip front, a single unverified report says Nvidia wants Samsung, Micron and SK hynix to build custom HBM base dies on TSMC's 3nm process, while a separate rumour suggests China could let major firms buy H200 chips under tight caps. Both remain unconfirmed.

Finance.title: AI selloff spreads to Asia as rates and oil bite
Finance.notification: Chip stocks post their longest losing run since 2008 as AI jitters and rate fears spread across Asia.
Finance.summary:
A sharp retreat in AI-linked shares is the dominant market story. US chip stocks have fallen for eight straight sessions, the longest run since 2008, and the Philadelphia semiconductor index is reported down about 16 percent. The selloff has spread to Asia's AI supply chain, with a Goldman Sachs basket of regional hardware names down 11 percent last week. Investors fear that rising borrowing costs could curb data-centre spending, while doubts about AI revenue, including a report that OpenAI's annualised revenue came in below estimates, have added to the unease.

Rates and energy are compounding the pressure. Inflation at 3.7 percent has led traders to price a high chance of another Fed hike this year, and US 10-year yields are described as above 5 percent for the first time in almost two decades. Oil is trading around US$108 to US$110 a barrel, with the Iran conflict and Strait of Hormuz disruption cited as key factors. Gold has risen to about US$4,181 an ounce.

Not all commentary is bleak. Several analysts describe the move as a recalibration of expectations rather than a broken AI story, and note that the next move may hinge on borrowing costs. Earnings from Meta, Tesla, Lam Research and Texas Instruments this week will be the next test.

points.text: SOXX closed about 14% below its October high after eight straight losing sessions, the longest run in 16 years.
UBS says the S&P 500 can absorb Fed hikes and expects hikes in December and March, a view it pairs with 28% Q3 EPS growth.
Indonesian stocks had their worst day since 1998 after MSCI warned it could downgrade the market.
France faces a possible bond sell-off after violent protests, with deficits above 5% of GDP and debt near 120%.
Zelenskiy says US intelligence-sharing with Ukraine has resumed after a pause; details of conditions are unclear.
Paris and other French cities saw riots and looting over high prices, with Carrefour reporting around 50 stores ransacked.

World.title: France unrest deepens as Macron faces pressure
World.notification: Riots and looting sweep French cities, with over 2,000 arrests and calls for the interior minister to resign.
World.summary:
France dominates the day's world news. Protests over living costs, school funding and public services turned violent over the weekend, with public buildings burned, shops looted and more than 2,000 people arrested. Reports cite around 1,500 businesses ransacked and about 1,000 police officers injured. The government held crisis talks, politicians from both sides have called for the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, to resign, and Macron addressed the nation calling for unity. Further union and gilets jaunes protests are planned for 5 November, with the presidential election about six months away. Markets have reacted with weakness in the CAC 40 and French bonds, and the episode is raising political risk in Europe's second-largest economy.

Unrest has spread beyond France. Cost-of-living and housing protests have reached Milan, Lisbon and Albania, where demonstrators in Tirana have clashed with police for six days and Prime Minister Edi Rama has refused to resign. Rama says the protests threaten Albania's EU path, and the Albanian unrest has been tied to a resort linked to Donald Trump's family.

Elsewhere, the Middle East and Ukraine remain volatile. Iran has hinted at a nuclear policy shift and set conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, supporting oil prices, while Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia drew a GCC condemnation. Ukraine's drone barrage of more than 1,000 drones on Russian oil sites, and Trump's pause on new Russia sanctions, add to energy-market uncertainty. A fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta, which has caused casualties, is also a major Canadian story.

points.text: Major fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta has caused deaths and injuries; cause still unconfirmed.

Tech.title: Microsoft reportedly exits Nscale's Essex AI site
Tech.notification: Microsoft reportedly pulls out of Nscale's Essex data centre weeks before its New York IPO.
Tech.summary:
The biggest tech story is the reported collapse of Microsoft's plan to anchor Nscale's Loughton data centre in Essex. The Telegraph reports Microsoft has ended the agreement, with grid officials reportedly saying power would not arrive until the 2030s. Nscale says it remains committed to the site, is exploring alternative power and sees its Microsoft relationship as strong. Microsoft has not commented.

The timing is awkward for Nscale, which has filed for a New York listing under the ticker NSCL with a flotation that could value it at up to $35bn. Microsoft and Anthropic together make up about 85% of its contracts, so the episode puts its delivery schedules under scrutiny. It also feeds wider investor caution around neocloud firms, with CoreWeave shares reported lower.

The broader backdrop is a sharp AI-trade selloff. Japanese chip stocks fell, Alphabet dropped on reports that its Gemini 3.5 Pro model is months behind, and OpenAI's $500bn Stargate project has reportedly hit obstacles, with its spending plans reportedly cut to $600bn through 2030. Musk's "Hardware is hard" jibe added to the scepticism. Investors are now looking to the Magnificent Seven earnings for reassurance on hyperscaler AI spending.

Chip news is mixed. Nvidia reportedly asked Samsung, SK hynix and Micron to use TSMC's 3nm process for custom memory base dies, and H200 sales to Chinese firms are reportedly moving forward under tight limits. Several of these items are unverified rumours and should be read with that in mind.

points.text: OpenAI's Stargate reportedly stalls, with spending plans cut to $600bn through 2030 from $1.4tn touted earlier.
Alphabet fell nearly 4.5% on reports Gemini 3.5 Pro is months behind schedule after weak coding results.

Samsung may reportedly switch to Exynos for the Galaxy S27 Ultra over overheating claims that Qualcomm denies.

Fashion.title: Paris looting hits luxury boutiques ahead of earnings
Fashion.notification: Paris unrest hit Burberry, Louis Vuitton and Dior boutiques as luxury groups head into earnings week.
Fashion.summary:
The biggest story is the violence in France, where cost-of-living protests turned into looting on Saturday. The Fédération du commerce et de la distribution estimates about 1,500 shops were affected, including luxury boutiques for Burberry, Louis Vuitton, Dior, Celine and Lacoste, and Sephora closed almost its whole French network. Retail bodies are calling for government action, Macron has condemned the violence, and unions have called a nationwide strike day for 5 November. Luxury shares fell on the news, and the timing is awkward because several groups report third-quarter earnings this week, with France a key market for LVMH and Hermès.

Elsewhere, the business backdrop looks uneven. Business of Fashion has flagged a difficult stretch for luxury, with weak numbers and empty chairs, and warned that the United States may be losing momentum as a source of demand. Chanel is pressing on in China with a first Wuhan store at SKP, due to sit on a pedestrian promenade alongside Louis Vuitton and Cartier, even as brands there close weak stores and test new regions.

Creative leadership is also in flux. Seán McGirr is leaving Alexander McQueen after three years, with his Spring/Summer 2027 London show as his last, and Veronica Leoni is reported to be exiting Calvin Klein. Both houses are now looking for new creative directors, a question that a New York Times piece has taken up.
